### Q1
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
# Data Overview
glimpse(ny_noaa)

# Check Missing Data
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    id_missing = sum(is.na(id)),
    date_missing = sum(is.na(date)),
    prcp_missing = sum(is.na(prcp)),
    snow_missing = sum(is.na(snow)),
    snwd_missing = sum(is.na(snwd)),
    tmax_missing = sum(is.na(tmax)),
    tmin_missing = sum(is.na(tmin))
  )
```
The ny_noaa dataset contains daily weather observations recorded at weather stations across New York State, with 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables: station ID, observation date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. Only station ID and observation date have no missing values, while all other variables contain substantial missing data. In particular, nearly half of the observations are missing temperature measurements. Since we do not know why these values are missing or whether there are any underlying patterns in the missingness, the missing temperature data may introduce bias into our overall assessment of climate conditions, potentially leading to overestimation or underestimation of temperature extremes.
```{r}
# Data Cleaning
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date)
  )

glimpse(ny_noaa)

# Snowfall Common Value
ny_noaa |>
  group_by(snow) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, which has 2,008,508 observations. This makes sense because the dataset includes observations throughout the year, and New York only expects snowfall in several winter days.
```{r}
# January and July Plots
noaa_temp = ny_noaa |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7)

noaa_temp = noaa_temp |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

noaa_temp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )
```
The plot shows a clear seasonal difference in average maximum temperatures between January and July. In January, average maximum temperatures fluctuate around 0°C, while in July, they generally range between 25°C and 30°C. This is reasonable given the natural temperature differences between winter and summer. Weather stations show similar year-to-year fluctuations within each month, with no obvious long-term increasing or decreasing trend. A few potential outliers can also be observed, particularly an unusually low temperature in January during the early 1980s and another unusually low temperature in July during the late 1980s.
```{r}
# Temperature Plot
# I first tried scatterplot, but the dataset was too large and R was stuck for nearly an hour. I then realized that it needs to be grouped into bins before plotting.
temp_plot = ny_noaa |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 40) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )
print(temp_plot)

# Snow Plot
snow_plot = ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  )
print(snow_plot)

# Two-panel Plot
temp_plot / snow_plot
```

### Q2
```{r}
# Loading
nhanes_covar = read_csv("nhanes_covar.csv")
glimpse(nhanes_covar)
# From glimpese the nhanes_covar dataset was not imported correctly bc the first four rows contain variable descriptions and were mistakenly interpreted as column names
nhanes_covar = read_csv("nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

nhanes_accel = read_csv("nhanes_accel.csv")
glimpse(nhanes_accel)

# Filtration
nhanes_covar = nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21)

nhanes_covar = nhanes_covar |>
  drop_na(sex, age, BMI, education)
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

# Mutation and Labelling
nhanes_covar = nhanes_covar |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("<high school", "=high school", ">high school")
    )
  )
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

# Merging
nhanes = nhanes_covar |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = "SEQN")
dim(nhanes)
```

```{r}
# Table of Sex and Education Level
nhanes_covartable = nhanes |>
  count(education, sex)

nhanes_covartable = nhanes_covartable |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

knitr::kable(
  nhanes_covartable,
  caption = "Number of Participants by Education Level and Sex"
)

# Age Distribution Visualization
nhanes |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Education Level",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```
The table shows that the >high school group has the largest number of participants among the three education categories. Within each education level, the numbers of males and females are relatively similar in the <high school group, while females slightly outnumber males in the >high school group. The most noticeable difference is observed in the =high school group, where there are considerably more males (35) than females (23).
The boxplot shows that participants in the <high school group have median ages around 60 years for both sexes, while in the =high school group, females have a obviously higher median age than males. Participants in the >high school group are generally younger, with median ages in the early 40s for both sexes. From the trend shown by this boxplot, higher education levels seems to be associated with younger ages.
```{r}
# Total Activities and Age Plot
# Convert from wide to long format first so can group by participant and sum their activity across all 1,440 minutes
nhanes_long = nhanes |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity"
  )
nhanes_activities = nhanes_long |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
dim(nhanes_activities)

nhanes_activities |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education Level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
In the <high school group, males and females show relatively similar activity patterns, with total activity decreasing as age increases. In the =high school group, females generally have higher total activity than males at younger ages, but this difference gradually becomes smaller with age. Within this group, total activity initially increases with age, reaches a peak, and then continues to decline. The >high school group shows a similar pattern: females generally have higher total activity at younger ages, but the gap gradually narrows as age increases.
Interestingly, all three groups show a similar "rebound" pattern, where total activity decreases until a certain age, suddenly increases to form a small peak, and then declines again. The reason behind this pattern might be worth further investigation.
Overall, total daily activity tends to decrease with age across all three education levels, although the trends are not entirely linear.
```{r}
# 24-hour Avtivities Plot
nhanes_long = nhanes_long |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min"))
  )
nhanes_time = nhanes_long |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_activity = mean(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
nhanes_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1440, by = 180),
    labels = paste0(seq(0, 24, by = 3), ":00")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns",
    x = "Time",
    y = "Mean Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
All three educational groups shown similar patterns of daily activity. Activity levels were lowest in the early morning, then rose rapidly and remained at a relatively high level during the day; gradually declined in the evening. The differences between male and female varied across the different educational groups. In the <high school group, the activity curves for male and female were relatively similar for most of the time; in the =high school group, female daytime activity levels were slightly higher than male; and in the >high school group, female daytime activity levels were significantly higher than male. There were also differences in activity levels among the different educational groups. The daytime peaks were relatively high in the <high school, while the daytime activity levels were slightly lower in the =high school and >high school group.

### Q3
```{r}
# Loading
jan2020 = read_csv("Jan 2020 Citi.csv")
glimpse(jan2020)
jul2020 = read_csv("July 2020 Citi.csv")
glimpse(jul2020)
jan2024 = read_csv("Jan 2024 Citi.csv")
glimpse(jan2024)
jul2024 = read_csv("July 2024 Citi.csv")
glimpse(jul2024)

# Binding and Cleaning
citibike = bind_rows(jan2020, jul2020, jan2024, jul2024)

citibike = citibike |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )
levels(citibike$weekdays)

# Add Years and Months
jan2020 = jan2020 |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

jul2020 = jul2020 |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

jan2024 = jan2024 |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

jul2024 = jul2024 |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )

citibike = bind_rows(jan2020, jul2020, jan2024, jul2024)
glimpse(citibike)

# Mutation
citibike = citibike |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual)
  )
glimpse(citibike)
```
This dataset contains Citi Bike ride data from January and July of 2020 and 2024, with a total of 99,485 observations and 9 variables: ride_id, rideable_type, weekdays, duration, start_station_name, end_station_name, member_casual, year, and month. Since the data were combined from four separate datasets, two variables year and month were added to label when each ride occurred. 43 rides have missing start station information, and 207 rides have missing end station information, but the proportion is very small to be excluded as NAs in later analyses if necessary.
```{r}
# Membership Table
citibike_table = citibike |>
  count(year, month, member_casual)

knitr::kable(
  citibike_table,
  caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Type"
)
# Current table shows all the information needed, but having year, month, and membership all mixed together makes each row a bit complicated to read. It might be clearer to separate membership types into different columns while keeping year and month as separate variables
citibike_comparison = citibike_table |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c(year, member_casual),
    values_from = n
  )

knitr::kable(
  citibike_comparison,
  caption = "Citi Bike Rides by Month, Year, and Membership Type"
)
```
Overall the number of rides increased substantially from 2020 to 2024 for both casual riders and members. In both years, members accounted for far more rides than casual riders,and both casual and member riders had considerably more rides in July than in January, which suggests that Citi Bike usage is much higher during the summer months. Interestingly the number of member rides in July 2024 (36,262) exceeded the total number of rides by both casual riders and members in July 2020 (21,048).
```{r}
# Popular Stations
citibike_july2024 = citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "July")

station_counts = citibike_july2024 |>
  filter(!is.na(start_station_name)) |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

station_counts

knitr::kable(
  station_counts,
  caption = "5 Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
)
```

```{r}
# My first thought was comparing each variable (week, month, year) to ride duration
# Weekday to Median Ride Duration
weekday_median = citibike |>
  group_by(weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
weekday_plot = weekday_median |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
weekday_plot

# Month to Median Ride Duration
month_median = citibike |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
month_plot = month_median |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = median_duration)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Month",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
month_plot

# Year to Median Ride Duration
year_median = citibike |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
year_plot = year_median |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = median_duration)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)"
  )
year_plot

weekday_plot / (month_plot | year_plot)
```
The three plots show some differences in median ride duration across weekdays, months, and years. For weekdays, median ride duration is relatively similar from Monday to Friday, while rides tend to last longer on weekends. For months, median ride duration is noticeably higher in July than in January. And surprisingly the median ride duration is higher in 2020 than in 2024, even though the number of rides increased substantially over this period.
```{r}
# These three plots compare each variable with median ride duration separately, without considering how weekday, month, and year interact. It would be better to create another plot that covers all three variables together
citibike_median = citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

citibike_median |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration,
             color = month, group = month)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  )
```
The most noticeable difference is between months. In both 2020 and 2024, median ride duration in July was much higher than in January. Comparing the two years, median ride duration in January changed very little, showing only a slight decrease from 2020 to 2024. But July showed a substantial decrease in median ride duration over the same period. Despite this decline, the overall weekday pattern remained similar, with longer rides on weekends than on weekdays.
(P.S. I got a little bit confused about what the difference really is between this plot and the three separate plots above. They seem to lead to pretty much the same conclusions to me?)
```{r}
# 2024 Distribution
citibike_2024 = citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024)

citibike_2024 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution in 2024",
    x = "Membership Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  )
```
Most rides in both January and July 2024 were relatively short, while only a small number of rides lasted a very long time, shown by the extreme long-tail on the plot. Casual riders generally had longer rides than members, especially when using classic bikes. Comparing bike types, classic bikes tended to have longer rides than electric bikes among casual riders, while the difference was less obvious among members.
